# Front passenger brake keeps sticking at random

A stuck caliper on a single axle, especially one generating enough heat to boil brake fluid or warp rotors, is a critical failure mode that demands more than just part swapping. The fact that you replaced the line, the caliper, and the master cylinder without resolving the issue suggests the root cause lies outside the standard "replace everything" checklist. Furthermore, the symptom of the problem returning immediately after reconnecting the ABS module provides a massive diagnostic clue: the hydraulic circuit is likely being modulated by the anti-lock braking system, or there is a mechanical binding that persists regardless of hydraulic pressure source.

When you disconnected the ABS and drove 20 miles with no issues, you effectively isolated the symptom to the interaction between the wheel cylinder assembly and the vehicle's electronic control logic. In modern vehicles like your 2007 Kia Sorento, the ABS modulator isn't just a passive pipe; it contains valves that open and close to pump pressure during hard stops or wheel speed discrepancies. If the front passenger caliper is sticking, it implies the piston is not retracting fully or is leaking internally. However, if disconnecting the ABS cures the heat generation temporarily, you must consider whether the modulator's solenoid valves are inadvertently holding pressure in that specific circuit during normal cruising, or if there is a mechanical interference preventing the caliper from sliding freely.

One common oversight when replacing a stuck caliper is ignoring the condition of the rear axle shafts or differential fluid temperature, though less likely to cause isolated front heat, it's worth noting. More pertinent here is the state of the brake line itself. You replaced the line, but was it a standard rubber hose or an upgraded steel braid? If the previous line had internal corrosion that wasn't fully flushed out before installing the new one, debris could still be lodged in the caliper bore. Additionally, ensure the bleeding process was thorough enough to remove any air introduced during the ABS disconnection/reconnection cycle. Air in the system can cause spongy feel, but trapped air under a stuck piston can also create hydraulic lock-up effects that mimic a mechanical stick.

Another angle is the physical mounting of the caliper. Did you inspect the guide pins and slide boots meticulously? If the slide pins are seized or the rubber boots are torn and allowing moisture ingress, the caliper will stick regardless of how clean the new piston is. It is easy to swap a brand-new caliper onto a frame that still retains rust buildup from the previous unit, effectively installing a perfect part on a compromised foundation. The mounting surface must be perfectly flat and free of pitting. If there is any residual corrosion on the bracket where the caliper slides, friction will increase to a point where the hydraulic pressure cannot overcome it during light braking events, leading to drag.

The ABS modulator valves themselves could be partially stuck open in that specific circuit. Even though the system is designed to isolate wheels, a faulty valve might not close completely, creating a constant low-level pressure build-up that keeps the piston engaged. This would explain why disconnecting the module fixed the issue temporarily; you removed the electronic modulation entirely, leaving only the static hydraulic state.

To diagnose this further without tearing into the ABS modulator immediately, perform a "static pressure test." With the wheel off and the caliper disconnected from the line, apply manual pressure to the piston (if possible) or simply inspect for internal scoring. If the piston moves freely but sticks when connected, the issue is hydraulic. If it sticks mechanically even with zero pressure applied, the focus must shift entirely to the slide pins and mounting bracket cleanliness.

Consider also checking the ABS control module logs if the vehicle has an OBD-II scanner capable of reading ABS-specific codes. While standard scanners often show only generic codes for a loose connection or low fluid, specialized tools can reveal if a specific wheel speed sensor is reporting erratic data that triggers the modulator to pump pressure repeatedly, creating heat even during coasting. If the sensor tone ring is dirty or damaged on that one wheel, the ECU might think the wheel is locking up and apply brakes constantly.

Before diving into expensive ABS component replacements, verify the integrity of the new brake line's flare and fitting torque. A slight misalignment at the caliper end can restrict flow enough to cause heat buildup over time. Ensure you are using the correct thread size and that the banjo bolt or flare nut is tightened to manufacturer specifications, not "finger tight" plus a guess. Precision matters when dealing with high-pressure hydraulic systems where a fraction of a millimeter in misalignment can drastically alter fluid dynamics.
